channel.description: Recent content in The terminal on Termorq

item.title: The prompt
item.description:
You type in one place, on the line after the latest output. The first characters decide what runs. The accent caret follows the insertion point as you edit the line. The folder is on the footer.

flowchart LR
 line["The line you type"]:::step
 shell["Shell"]:::out
 endpoint["@endpoint"]:::step
 tool["@tool"]:::store
 skill["/ skill"]:::gate
 model{"@chat # @agent"}:::gate

 line --> shell
 line --> endpoint
 line --> tool
 line --> skill
 line --> model

 classDef store fill:#134e4a,stroke:#5eead4,stroke-width:2px,color:#f4fbfa
 classDef gate fill:#FFC131,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:2px,color:#1a1404
 classDef step fill:#0f766e,stroke:#99f6e4,stroke-width:2px,color:#f4fbfa
 classDef out fill:#155e75,stroke:#67e8f9,stroke-width:2px,color:#f4fbfa
 linkStyle 0,2 stroke:#5eead4,stroke-width:2.5px
 linkStyle 1 stroke:#67e8f9,stroke-width:2.5px
 linkStyle 3,4 stroke:#FFC131,stroke-width:2.5px
You type What runs
git status The tab’s shell. Output streams in. cd and export carry to the next line on bash, zsh, sh, and PowerShell
@endpoint List users A saved HTTP call
@tool search --query tea An MCP tool on a server connected to this tab
/explain how to make tea A skill from skills.yaml
@chat why was that empty? The tab’s model, with recent scrollback. It can call this tab’s MCP tools and saved endpoints; you approve each call
Agent on, then why was that empty? The same chat, without typing @chat. A line that starts with @ still runs
# find files over 100 MB here The model writes one command into the prompt. You press Enter
@history The history overlay for this tab

@ opens the commands palette. / opens the skills palette. Both filter as you type. In the commands palette, exact and leading name matches appear before other name matches, and all name matches appear before description matches. Built-in @ actions are listed in Commands. Entries from commands.yaml follow them. @history is always first and is not a YAML entry.

item.title: Shells
item.description:
A line that is not an @ command or a / skill runs in the tab’s shell. One command runs at a time per tab. Output streams in while it runs. Ctrl+C stops that command and everything it started.

Which shells link

Settings → Shell picks the shell for every tab that has not chosen its own, from the ones installed here.

item.title: Tabs and splits
item.description:
Each tab is its own session: scrollback, folder, history, MCP servers, and OpenAI connection. Switching tabs leaves a running command where it is.

Add, rename, close link

+ adds a tab in the start folder. Right-click for Rename and Change colour. Middle-click, ×, or Close removes the tab. Closing the last tab resets it.

item.title: Interactive terminal
item.description:
Most lines are non-interactive: the app starts the shell, streams the output, and returns to the prompt. A program that needs a keyboard opens a pseudo-terminal in the tab instead. On Windows that terminal is ConPTY. The screen is drawn with xterm.js.

These open a terminal on their own:

item.title: History and plain English
item.description:
Command history link

↑ and ↓ cycle the commands on this tab when no palette is open. The app keeps the last 500 in command_history.json in the app data folder. Each entry is the command and at, Unix epoch milliseconds. An older file that was a plain list of strings is migrated on load (at: 0 shows as an unknown time).

item.title: Find and export
item.description:
Open links and files from output link

URLs and file paths in command output have a dotted underline. Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on macOS) opens a URL in the browser, or a file in its default app. Add Shift to show the file in Finder, Explorer, or the file manager instead. Relative paths such as src/App.tsx:12 are found from the tab’s folder, and ~/ is the home folder. A plain click still selects text. Only http and https links open.

item.title: Drop-down window
item.description:
The drop-down window is a Quake-style terminal. A global shortcut shows Termorq from the top of the screen, wherever you are, and the same shortcut hides it.

Turn it on link

Open Settings → Drop-down window and switch it On. It is off by default.

Setting Default What it does
Shortcut Cmd+Shift+Space on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+Space on Windows and Linux The global key. Click the button, then press the new combination. Esc keeps the old one

A shortcut needs Ctrl, Alt or Cmd. A bare key or Shift alone is refused, because it would take ordinary typing away from every app. If another app already owns the combination, Settings shows the error and nothing is registered.

item.title: Markdown runbooks
item.description:
Markdown runbooks are a Pro feature. In Free, @md, the md palette entry, and dropping a .md file show Markdown runbooks are available in the Pro edition. See Editions.

A runbook is often a Markdown file: a few sentences, then a command. Termorq opens that file and lets you run each code block where you read it.

Open a file link

Type @md and press Enter. A file dialog asks for a .md file.

item.title: Recording and replay
item.description:
Session recording is a Pro feature (terminal.session_recording in features.yml). In the Free edition, Start recording, @record and the palette entry show “Record and replay a tab session is available in the Pro edition.” instead, and replaying a .cast is Pro too.

A recording keeps a tab’s commands and output with their timing, in the asciinema v2 .cast format. Play it back in Termorq or with asciinema play.

item.title: Inline images
item.description:
Termorq draws images where a terminal or an API sends them. Settings → Inline images turns it on or off. It is on by default.

Shell output link

Programs that use the iTerm2 inline image protocol draw in the scrollback. For example, with iTerm2’s imgcat script:

imgcat ~/Pictures/diagram.png

The image appears in place of the escape sequence. Only images marked inline=1 are drawn. A file transfer without it is dropped.
